## Engineering Context

The assigned armature geometry and loading are not inferred from this photograph.](assets/dinosaur-tail-curved-industry-context.png){fig-alt="Museum gallery containing mounted dinosaur skeletons; an elevated dinosaur tail appears in the background." width="92%"}

A museum engineering team must conceal a curved steel armature within an elevated sauropod tail. Vertebrae and mounting cradles diminish toward the tip, so the assigned total gravity intensity decreases linearly along the armature. The model represents a preliminary teaching analysis, not the photographed skeleton or a certified exhibit design.

## Components and Load Path

- mounted vertebrae and cradles transfer gravity load into the concealed armature;
- the curved hollow steel armature carries axial force, shear, and bending;
- an equivalent fixed pelvis-region mounting frame restrains the root;
- the main exhibit support and floor carry the root reactions into the building.

## Assigned Mechanics Model

Use a planar circular-arc centerline with

$$x(\theta)=R\sin\theta,\qquad y(\theta)=R(1-\cos\theta),\qquad s=R\theta,$$

from $\theta=0$ at the fixed root to $\theta=\theta_t$ at the free tip. Analyze section S at $\theta=\theta_S$. The total downward load per unit **arc length** is

$$q(\theta)=q_0+\frac{q_t-q_0}{\theta_t}\theta,$$

and already includes steel self-weight. Therefore, do not add self-weight again.

For the required integrations, use $ds=R\,d\theta$ and the formulas supplied in the mechanics questions. At S, the local unit vectors are $\mathbf e_t=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $\mathbf e_n=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$.

## Scope and Provenance

The radius, angles, load intensities, tube geometry, material properties, and required factor of safety are physically reasoned instructional assumptions. They were not measured from the photograph. The section is a teaching geometry, not a verified stocked product. Use curved-centerline equilibrium and an ordinary axial-plus-flexure stress approximation appropriate to a slender member. Do not apply classical tight-radius curved-beam theory or a straight-cantilever deflection formula.
